hints: Focus on what forming a nitrile does to the carbon chain, the CN carbon becomes part of the product name.
Pentanenitrile has 5 carbons in total, so the starting bromoalkane must have one carbon fewer, that is 4 carbons.
Recall which cyanide reagent actually supplies CN- for substitution, and why alcoholic conditions are needed for a halogenoalkane.
walkthrough:
**Work out what pentanenitrile looks like**

Pentanenitrile is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Count carefully, it has 5 carbons in total.

Remember the rule:
$$\text{nitrile carbons} = \text{halogenoalkane carbons} + 1$$

**Find the right carbon chain length**

To get 5 carbons in the nitrile, you must start from a 4-carbon bromoalkane, that is 1-bromobutane.

Rows A and B show the shorter 4-carbon chain, while rows C and D show a longer 5-carbon chain which would give hexanenitrile.

**Choose the correct cyanide reagent**

Substitution of Br by CN- needs a good source of cyanide ions:
$$\text{R-Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{R-CN} + \text{Br}^-$$
$\text{KCN}$ in ethanol provides free $\text{CN}^-$ and is the standard reagent. $\text{HCN}$ is a weak acid, mostly undissociated, so it does not work for halogenoalkanes.

**Put both clues together**

You need the 4-carbon bromoalkane plus heat with $\text{KCN}$ in ethanol. That combination gives:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{KCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{KBr}$$

options.A: The carbon chain is correct (4-carbon bromoalkane would give a 5-carbon nitrile), but the reagent is wrong. HCN is a weak acid and provides very little CN-, so no nucleophilic substitution occurs. HCN is used for addition to aldehydes and ketones, not for halogenoalkanes.
options.B: This has both correct parts. The 4-carbon 1-bromobutane gains one carbon from CN- to give 5-carbon pentanenitrile, and KCN in ethanol provides CN- for nucleophilic substitution on heating.
options.C: Two problems here. The reagent HCN does not supply CN- for substitution, and the starting material is a 5-carbon 1-bromopentane, which would give a 6-carbon nitrile (hexanenitrile) even if KCN were used.
options.D: The reagent KCN in ethanol is correct for nitrile formation, but the carbon count is wrong. Starting from 5-carbon 1-bromopentane adds one more carbon to give hexanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, not pentanenitrile.
